TO THE HONORABLE SAMUEL A. ALITO, JR., ASSOCIATE JUSTICE OF 
THE SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES AND CIRCUIT JUSTICE 
FOR THE FIFTH CIRCUIT:
Pursuant to Rule 23 of the Rules of this Court and the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. 
§ 1651, applicants the City of Baltimore, et al., respectfully apply for a stay of the 
judgment entered on June 22, 2026, by the United States District Court for the 
Northern District of Texas (App. 49a-50a), pending the consideration and disposition 
of their appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit and, if the 
court of appeals affirms, pending the timely filing and disposition of a petition for a 
writ of certiorari and any further proceedings in this Court.
Four members of this Court recently noted that a “host of important questions” 
arise when the federal government seeks to evade the strictures of the Administrative 
Procedure Act (APA) through “‘rulemaking-by-collusive acquiescence.’” Arizona v. 
City & County of San Francisco, 596 U.S. 763, 766 (2022) (Roberts, C.J., concurring, 
joined by Thomas, Alito, & Gorsuch, JJ.) (quoting City & County of San Francisco v. 
U.S. Citizenship and Immigr. Servs., 992 F.3d 742, 744 (9th Cir. 2021) (VanDyke, J., 
dissenting)). A new administration hostile to a regulation promulgated by its 
predecessor can leverage litigation brought by an ideologically aligned party “to 
circumvent the usual and important requirement, under the Administrative 
Procedure Act, that a regulation originally promulgated using notice and comment 
. . . may only be repealed through notice and comment.” Id.; see also Danco Labs., 
LLC v. All. for Hippocratic Med., 143 S. Ct. 1075 (2023) (Alito, J., dissenting) 
(highlighting that it “has become the practice” for agencies to “leverag[e]” district

2
court injunctions to “implement[] a desired policy while evading both necessary 
agency procedures and judicial review”).
This case involves an egregious new extension of this phenomenon. The 
government did not merely leverage a convenient loss to undo agency action, but 
rather, announced in advance that it would not defend a disfavored regulation and 
then colluded with the challenger from the moment that suit was filed. The result is 
that a significant regulation that established certain important procedures in
immigration courts was erased over the course of a single day, without meaningful 
judicial review, public participation, or adherence to the APA’s rulemaking 
requirements.
The regulation in question, Efficient Case and Docket Management in 
Immigration Proceedings, 89 Fed. Reg. 46742 (May 29, 2024) (the Rule), was issued 
by the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) after a full notice-andcomment process enabled the public to participate in the rulemaking. Among other 
things, the Rule codified a preexisting practice under which immigration judges had 
discretion to administratively close immigration proceedings when doing so would 
promote efficiency or protect due process rights. Thus, for example, a crime victim or 
neglected juvenile with a credible pending application for affirmative relief before 
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) could be spared having to defend 
themselves in a removal proceeding while simultaneously undergoing the often 
lengthy USCIS adjudication process.

3
Administrative closure has existed in some form for decades. See, e.g., GarciaDeLeon v. Garland, 999 F.3d 986, 989 (6th Cir. 2021). But the practice has become
controversial, with critics describing it as facilitating a form of de facto amnesty. After 
the change in administration, EOIR’s new Acting Director issued a policy 
memorandum endorsing these criticisms and stating that EOIR would not defend the 
Final Rule against legal challenge. App. 107a. But EOIR did not then undertake the 
process contemplated by 5 U.S.C. § 553 for repealing an agency regulation. 
Instead, Texas challenged the Rule in the Wichita Falls Division of the 
Northern District of Texas, and the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) immediately 
joined in a motion to have final judgment entered in Texas’s favor. In so doing, DOJ
chose to forgo available jurisdictional and remedial arguments that the government
routinely raises when confronted with similar challenges to even those federal 
regulations it declines to defend on the merits. The joint motion even expressly
acknowledged that DOJ was asking for a form of relief—universal vacatur—that it 
regularly argues is legally unavailable, but which DOJ said it would accept here. And 
in a sharp departure from longstanding DOJ practice, DOJ also asked that the rule 
not only be vacated, but that a permanent injunction be entered that would bar the 
agency from ever adopting any similar regulation in the future. Cf. Horne v. Flores, 
557 U.S. 433, 449 (2009) (“consent decrees present a risk of collusion between 
advocacy groups and executive officials who want to bind the hands of future 
policymakers”). The district court entered the consent judgment, including the 
requested permanent injunction, on the same day suit was filed. The court also

4
vacated the Rule nationwide and in its entirety, even though Texas had only 
challenged the legality of the Rule’s administrative closure provisions and the Rule 
contains both provisions addressing separate issues and an express severability 
clause. 
Applicants are three municipalities with large immigrant populations 
(Baltimore, Maryland; Columbus, Ohio; and New Haven, Connecticut) (“the Cities”)
and one legal services provider (Centro Legal de la Raza) that promptly sought to 
intervene to provide the defense of the Rule that the nominal defendants failed to 
offer. The Cities based their standing allegations on precisely the same logic that 
Texas invoked when asserting its own standing. Texas had alleged that 
administrative closure prevents the removal of noncitizens, whose continued 
presence inflicts financial costs on the state. The Cities explained that the same
removals Texas alleged would necessarily follow from the judgment will encompass 
some of the Cities’ taxpayers. The Cities further explained that vacatur of the Rule 
undermines the protections conferred by U visa certifications, which the Cities’ law 
enforcement arms use to secure cooperation from immigrant crime victims. Centro 
Legal, in turn, explained that the consent judgment will necessitate its performance 
of unfunded legal work and erases a litigation victory that Centro Legal had obtained 
in a challenge to an earlier EOIR regulation that had been rescinded by the Rule.
The district court nonetheless denied intervention solely on the theory that 
each intervenor lacks Article III standing. The district court concluded the Cities’ 
allegations of harm were speculative, even though the Cities had merely asked the

5
court to credit the very allegations Texas itself had made in support of its own 
standing. The district court never attempted to reconcile its conclusion that the Cities 
did not have standing with the court’s implicit conclusion that Texas did have 
standing on the very same logic—a conclusion necessary to the district court’s 
decision to enter judgment on the merits in the case. 
Applicants appealed from both the denial of their intervention motion and the
underlying consent judgment, and that appeal remains pending. They promptly 
sought a stay of the consent judgment pending appeal, but that motion was denied 
by the Fifth Circuit without written opinion.
This Court has previously stayed a district court order vacating an agency 
policy when putative intervenors (including Texas) were seeking to establish their 
right to defend that policy in the federal government’s stead. See Arizona v. 
Mayorkas, 143 S. Ct. 478 (2022) (per curiam). The same relief is warranted here, 
especially given the dramatic consequences that the district court’s judgment 
invalidating the Rule will have on practice in the immigration courts with 
implications for “hundreds of thousands” of cases. App. 4a. This Court often grants a 
stay when a single district court vacates a significant federal policy nationwide. The 
situation here is more extreme because it is unclear whether even one judge has found 
the Rule unlawful after an independent merits analysis. See Mi Familia Vota v. 
Fontes, 152 F.4th 1153, 1156 (9th Cir. 2025) (R. Nelson, J., dissenting) (explaining 
that “a court may enter a consent decree against a government defendant without 
finding that a statutory or constitutional violation has occurred”) (citation and

6
quotation marks omitted). At a minimum, the vacatur here was issued by a district 
court that did not have the benefit of adversarial presentation before entering a
consent judgment on the same day suit was filed. 
The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this 
suit from its inception. This Court has long recognized the dangers of “friendly suit[s]” 
between nominal adversaries pursuing a shared goal, which both offend Article III 
and expose courts to being “misled into doing grievous harm to the public” by striking 
down legislative acts “upon agreed and general statements.” Chicago & G.T. Ry. Co. 
v. Wellman, 143 U.S. 339, 346 (1892). If a judgment procured through such open 
collusion is allowed to remain in effect, any agency can avoid the strictures of the 
APA by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by 
immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief. As long as this judgment serves as a 
viable template, this Court’s holding that agencies must “use the same procedures 
when they amend or repeal a rule as they used to issue the rule in the first instance” 
will be effectively a dead letter. See Perez v. Mortg. Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. 92, 101
(2015). And given agency incentives, such collusive suits will surely proliferate
further. 
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. The Administrative Closure Rule
Like federal courts, immigration courts have tools to manage their crowded 
dockets efficiently. One tool, known as administrative closure, operates to suspend 
removal proceedings in certain circumstances. See, e.g., 8 C.F.R. § 1003.18(c)

7
(defining administrative closure as the “temporary suspension of a case”). This 
practice is longstanding. See, e.g., Garcia-DeLeon, 999 F.3d at 989 (“For at least three 
decades, immigration judges and the [Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)] regularly 
administratively closed cases.”). In the Rule, EOIR used notice-and-comment 
procedures to adopt a regulatory framework governing administrative closure. DOJ 
invoked its rulemaking authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 
8 U.S.C. § 1103(g)(2).
The Rule authorizes administrative closure under certain conditions. See 8 
C.F.R. § 1003.18(c)(3); id. § 1003.1(l). One such circumstance is when a noncitizen 
has a pending application for relief before USCIS, a separate agency. In 
circumstances where such relief would “provide the noncitizen with legal status or 
some other basis that would prevent enforcing an order of removal, thus eliminating 
the need for further removal proceedings,” administrative closure can promote 
efficiency by “reducing the immediate need to conclude removal proceedings.” 89 Fed. 
Reg. at 46745. But even if a case is administratively closed, the adjudicator can 
recalendar the case (i.e., resume proceedings) upon a party’s motion. 8 C.F.R. 
§ 1003.18(c); id. § 1003.1(l)(2).
The Rule also adopted distinct changes to immigration court and BIA 
procedures. One procedure, known as termination, allows for disposition of a case in 
certain circumstances, including where the noncitizen has obtained lawful status

8 
through a U visa.1 See 8 C.F.R. § 1003.18(d); id. § 1003.1(m). Other provisions 
addressed the background check process for noncitizens, briefing schedules before the 
BIA, and the BIA’s authority to reopen cases sua sponte. 89 Fed. Reg. at 46743, 
46766-67. Each of these other changes functioned independently from the 
administrative closure provisions, as the Rule’s express severability clause makes 
clear. Id. at 46786.
The Rule also largely rescinded an earlier EOIR regulation, Appellate 
Procedures and Decisional Finality in Immigration Proceedings; Administrative 
Closure, 85 Fed. Reg. 81588 (Dec. 16, 2020) (“the 2020 Rule”), which would have 
restricted administrative closure. The 2020 Rule was also adopted after notice-andcomment rulemaking. See Appellate Procedures and Decisional Finality in 
Immigration Proceedings; Administrative Closure, 85 Fed. Reg. 52491 (Aug. 26, 2020)
(proposed rule). As discussed below, the 2020 Rule was preliminarily enjoined shortly 
after its issuance in a suit brought by Centro Legal. See 89 Fed. Reg. at 46742. 
After the change in administration, EOIR’s Acting Director issued a policy 
memorandum stating that EOIR “could not—and will not—defend the [Rule] in good 
faith against legal challenge.” App. 107a. EOIR did not initiate the rulemaking that 
5 U.S.C. § 553 requires to rescind a regulation.
1 U nonimmigrant status, commonly known as a U visa, is available to certain crime victims 
who aid law enforcement in investigating or prosecuting crimes. See generally 8 U.S.C. 
§§ 1101(a)(15)(U), 1184(p); 8 C.F.R. § 214.14.

9
B. Procedural History
1. The complaint and same-day consent judgment. Nearly two years after 
the Rule’s adoption, Texas filed suit, alleging that the Rule exceeds the agency’s 
statutory authority. App. 1a-43a. Texas claimed standing on the theory that the 
Rule’s administrative closure provisions permit undocumented individuals “to 
remain indefinitely in the United States by administrative closure rather than having 
their cases adjudicated to completion, and removed.” App. 25a. Texas averred that 
vacatur of the Rule would “necessarily reduce the number of cases administratively 
closed and, therefore, reduce the number of illegal aliens permitted to remain 
indefinitely in the United States.” App. 27a.
Within hours, and before any summons issued or DOJ had even noticed an 
appearance, the parties jointly moved for entry of a consent judgment. The joint 
motion asked the court to declare the Rule unlawful and vacate it, and to permanently 
enjoin DOJ from enforcing the Rule or promulgating similar regulations in the future. 
App. 44a-47a. The motion did not engage with the Rule’s legal justifications; it simply 
recited that “[t]he Parties agree” that the Rule authorizes “indefinite administrative 
closure without legal justification” and “further agree” that the Rule “was 
inadequately justified under the circumstances and was arbitrary and capricious.” 
App. 45a-46a. While DOJ joined the motion in full, it included a footnote stating its 
position that the APA does not authorize a court to vacate an agency rule, but that 
DOJ nonetheless “agrees not to pursue this position in this case.” App. 45a.

10
That same day, the district court entered the consent judgment. It vacated the 
“Administrative Closure Rule”—defined as the entire Rule, including those portions 
distinct from administrative closure—nationwide. App. 49a-50a. It declared that “no 
statute authorizes immigration judges to indefinitely administratively close or 
suspend adjudication of a case before them.” App. 49a. It permanently enjoined 
Defendants from enforcing the Rule and from promulgating any regulation 
permitting immigration judges to administratively close proceedings “without 
reaching the merits of a case absent an express statutory basis to do so.” App. 50a.
And it recorded the parties’ waiver of “any right to appeal.” Id.
2. The motion to intervene. Within the period for noticing a timely appeal, 
Applicants moved to intervene for the purpose of appealing the consent judgment. 
App. 87a.
The Cities: Baltimore, Columbus, and New Haven are local governments with 
substantial immigrant populations. App. 73a, 76a, 81a. They explained that if, as 
Texas avers, the judgment will result in more deportations of noncitizens across the 
United States, it will predictably impair the Cities’ municipal income-tax revenue 
because their taxpayers will be deported. App. 53a, 81a-82a. Moreover, the judgment 
undermines public safety by stripping certified U visa applicants of protection against 
removal, predictably making noncitizens less willing to cooperate with law 
enforcement. App. 82a-83a.
Centro Legal: Centro Legal represents noncitizens facing removal 
proceedings, including between 80 and 100 noncitizens with cases that have been

11
administratively closed. App. 63a. Recalendaring those cases would impose 
substantial uncompensated legal work on Centro Legal. App. 63a-70a. Also, Centro 
Legal was a lead plaintiff in a challenge to the 2020 Rule that would have similarly 
restricted administrative closure, and it obtained a preliminary injunction against 
that rule’s enforcement. See Centro Legal de la Raza v. EOIR, 524 F. Supp. 3d 919 
(N.D. Cal. 2021). The parties to that case stipulated to dismissal once the Rule 
rescinded the 2020 Rule, on the understanding that the 2020 Rule would not take 
effect and administrative closure would remain available. See Centro Legal de la Raza 
v. EOIR, No. 3:21-cv-00463 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 10, 2025), Dkt. No. 109.
3. The decisions below. The district court denied intervention solely on the 
theory that no Applicant has Article III standing, rendering intervention “futile.” 
App. 88a-94a. It did not address any of the requirements of Federal Rule of Civil 
Procedure 24. See App. 94a. As principally relevant here, the district court concluded 
the Cities’ harms from the consent judgment were too attenuated to support standing 
because the judgment at most would lead to recalendaring of administratively closed 
cases, but that the federal government would continue to “exercise discretion to 
enforce any resulting removal order,” such that the Rule would not necessarily lead 
to the removal of any of the Cities’ taxpayers or of crime victims cooperating with the 
Cities’ law enforcement agencies. App. 91a. The district court offered no explanation 
why that same logic would not undermine Texas’s assertion of standing, given that 
redress of its alleged injuries depends on the actual removal of noncitizens. The court 
also decided that, under Fifth Circuit precedent, Centro Legal lacked standing as a

12
nonprofit legal-services provider whose business activities would be affected by the 
judgment. App. 93a. 
Applicants timely appealed both the denial of intervention and the underlying 
consent judgment. See, e.g., Mausolf v. Babbitt, 125 F.3d 661, 666 (8th Cir. 1997)
(explaining that party denied intervention can file a protective notice of appeal from 
the judgment in the underlying suit). Both the district court (App. 95a) and the court 
of appeals (App. 99a) denied stays of the consent judgment pending appeal. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW
A stay is warranted when there are: (1) “a reasonable probability” that this 
Court would eventually grant certiorari on the question presented in the stay 
application, (2) a fair prospect that the Court will reverse the decision below, and (3) a 
likelihood that irreparable harm will result from the denial of a stay. Hollingsworth 
v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010). The Court also considers whether a stay would 
substantially injure the other parties interested in the proceedings and whether it 
would serve the public interest. Ohio v. EPA, 603 U.S. 279, 291 (2024).
REASONS FOR GRANTING THE STAY
I. THERE IS A REASONABLE PROBABILITY THAT THIS COURT WILL 
EVENTUALLY GRANT CERTIORARI 
A. This Court Has Previously Granted Certiorari to Address the 
Important Questions Posed by Rulemaking Through Collusive 
Acquiescence and Is Reasonably Likely to Do So Again Here
1. This Court has repeatedly recognized in recent years the important and 
certiorari-worthy questions that arise when the federal government ceases defending 
its own regulatory action and other affected parties seek to intervene post-judgment

13
to provide that defense. See Arizona v. City & County of San Francisco, 142 S. Ct. 417 
(2021); Arizona v. Mayorkas, 143 S. Ct. 478 (2022). Yet, this Court has been frustrated 
from providing needed clarification on this issue, which is squarely presented here. 
There is thus at least a reasonable probability that this Court will grant certiorari.
In City & County of San Francisco, this Court granted certiorari to answer the 
question: “Whether States with interests should be permitted to intervene to defend 
a rule when the United States ceases to defend.” Pet. for Cert., No. 20-1775 (June 23, 
2021) (S.F. Pet.); see also Arizona v. City & County of San Francisco, 142 S. Ct. 417 
(2021) (granting certiorari limited to the first question raised in the petition). Further 
developments in the case ultimately prevented the Court from reaching the issue. See 
Arizona v. City & County of San Francisco, 596 U.S. 763 (2022) (per curiam). But four 
members of this Court emphasized that a “host of important questions” remain 
unresolved regarding the appropriate treatment of cases involving rulemaking by 
collusive acquiescence. Id. at 766 (Roberts, C.J., concurring, joined by Thomas, Alito, 
& Gorsuch, JJ.). Likewise, in Mayorkas, this Court stayed a district court’s vacatur 
and granted certiorari to decide whether intervention should be allowed postjudgment to defend a policy the federal government sought to terminate, but again, 
subsequent developments led to the case being dismissed before the merits could be 
decided. Arizona v. Mayorkas, 143 S. Ct. 1312 (2023).
There is a substantial continuing need for this Court to address whether
litigation tactics can be substituted for the APA’s requirement that a federal 
regulation adopted through notice-and-comment rulemaking may be rescinded only

14
through notice-and-comment rulemaking. Mortg. Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. at 101.
Courts have long held that an agency may not “circumvent” its notice-and-comment 
obligations “merely by confessing that the regulations were defective in some 
respect.” Consumer Energy Council of Am. v. FERC, 673 F.2d 425, 447 n.79 (D.C. Cir. 
1982), aff’d, 463 U.S. 1216 (1983). Texas, for its part, has told this Court that the 
question is certiorari-worthy and that the federal government cannot end-run the 
APA by “drop[ping] its litigation defenses and acquiesc[ing] to a final substantive 
judgment against it, especially one vacating its rule.” Br. for Pet. at 12, Arizona v. 
City & County of San Francisco, No. 20-1775 (U.S. Dec. 13, 2021) (citation omitted)
(S.F. Br.); see also Application for Stay at 2, Arizona v. Mayorkas, No. 22A544 (Dec. 
19, 2022).
Yet, the practice of regulatory repeal by acquiescence has become increasingly 
common and effective. See Danco Labs., 143 S. Ct. at 1076 (Alito, J., dissenting). The 
transition between the Biden and Trump administrations has not brought any 
slowdown in the practice. See, e.g., John Lewis & Aaron Baum, Trump’s Use of 
Consent Decrees to Dismantle Policy, Just Security (Sept. 23, 2025),
https://www.justsecurity.org/121057/trump-consent-decrees-dismantle-policy/
(collecting examples). Indeed, this case illustrates that the practice of regulatory 
repeal by consent decree is not merely continuing apace but taking new and even 
more troubling forms. In both City & County of San Francisco and Mayorkas, the 
government’s acquiescence came only after a rule had been litigated and judgments

15
entered against it. Here, the federal government never even attempted to defend the 
Rule.
The egregious collusion in this case makes it a particularly compelling 
candidate for certiorari, should the court of appeals affirm the district court. Texas 
sued more than two years after the Rule was issued and only after the federal 
government announced that it “could not—and will not—defend” the Rule “against 
legal challenge.” App. 107a. On the day Texas sued in the Wichita Falls Division of 
the Northern District of Texas, the parties jointly asked the sole district judge 
assigned to that division for identical relief. App. 44a-47a; see Special Order No. 3-
343 (N.D. Tex. Sept. 14, 2022). DOJ reaffirmed its belief that the APA does not 
authorize universal vacatur, yet it told the district court that it “agrees not to pursue 
this position in this case,” while reserving “the right to continue to advance this 
position in other cases.” App. 45a n.1. Nor did it challenge Texas’s standing, though 
Texas’s theory of injury closely resembles the one this Court rejected in United States 
v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670 (2023). And DOJ sought and obtained a permanent injunction 
that would prevent a future administration from seeking to reinstitute 
administrative closure—despite DOJ’s long recognition of the grave problems that 
arise from entering into court orders that indefinitely bind future administrations. 
Cf. Memorandum from Edwin Meese III, Att’y Gen., to All Assistant Att’ys Gen. & 
All U.S. Att’ys 3 (Mar. 13, 1986).
2. In opposing the stay motion in the court of appeals, the parties took the 
position that the denial of intervention created a threshold issue that would insulate

16
the consent judgment from substantive review. But cases involving the collusive 
settlement of APA claims are unavoidably bound up in questions of whether putative 
intervenors should be allowed to intervene. If intervention is never sought (or, as 
here, not permitted), the collusive settlement or acquiescence will remain 
unchallenged. And if intervention is successful, the most troubling aspects of the 
collusion are mitigated because the intervenor will offer the defense and adversity 
that the federal government has not provided. It should therefore be unsurprising 
that both City & County of San Francisco and Mayorkas reached this Court after 
denials of intervention. 
This case would provide the Court with a suitable vehicle to reiterate that 
intervention supplies a critical safeguard against collusive “hobbled litigation rather 
than a full and fair adversarial testing” of a case and, thus, should generally be 
allowed to the maximum extent consistent with Article III when there is risk of 
collusion. Berger v. N.C. State Conf. of the NAACP, 597 U.S. 179, 191-92 (2022). All 
reasonable factual inferences should be drawn in favor of intervention. As Texas itself 
recently explained, “[t]he only way to check norm-breaking actions” from regulatory 
repeal through acquiescence “is by allowing parties who would be injured by a judicial 
invalidation to intervene once the Government stops defending the rule.” S.F. Br. 39.
The facts supporting intervention here are particularly compelling because the 
Cities’ injuries closely mirror Texas’s, meaning any determination that the Cities lack 
standing only casts doubt on the validity of the underlying judgment. Texas’s suit 
hinged on its assertion that vacatur “will necessarily . . . reduce the number of illegal

17
aliens permitted to remain indefinitely in the United States.” App. 27a. As Applicants
explained, if widespread removals will “necessarily” follow from the consent
judgment, their residents (including taxpaying immigrants with work 
authorizations) predictably will be affected. If Texas’s stake in the Rule’s vacatur was 
concrete enough to support a judgment, Applicants’ stake in its survival is concrete 
enough to support intervention.
B. The Question of Whether Administrative Closure Is Statutorily 
Authorized Is Independently Worthy of Certiorari
This Court is also likely to grant certiorari on the substantive question resolved 
in the consent judgment: whether the Rule is contrary to law. Whether the Attorney 
General may provide for administrative closure is an “important question of federal 
law that has not been, but should be, settled by this Court.” Sup. Ct. R. 10(c). By the 
parties’ own account, the practice has reached hundreds of thousands of cases. See
App. 46a (quoting Hernandez-Serrano v. Barr, 981 F.3d 459, 465 (6th Cir. 2020)). And

administrative closure. Meza Morales v. Barr, 973 F.3d 656, 667 (7th Cir. 2020)

18
expressly, as the Rule did. See infra Part II.B.3. No court of appeals has held what

This Court’s review is needed now because the consent judgment permanently 
bars the government from authorizing administrative closure by regulation “absent 
an express statutory basis to do so.” App. 50a. The parties have waived appeal. Id.
Under the consent judgment, no new rule can issue for another court to review, and 
no party to the judgment can appeal the district court’s decision. If this Court does 
not decide the question, the longstanding practice of administrative closure will be 
effectively precluded without full review.
II. APPLICANTS ARE LIKELY TO SUCCEED ON THE MERITS
There is more than a fair prospect that this Court would reverse the denial of 
intervention and vacate the consent judgment. The denial of intervention cannot be 
reconciled with the consent judgment, and the consent judgment was entered without 
a genuine case or controversy, in circumvention of the APA, on an erroneous view of 
the law, and with overbroad relief.
A. The Denial of Intervention Is Likely to Be Reversed
The district court denied intervention solely on the ground that it would be 
futile because Applicants lack Article III standing. App. 88a-92a. Under Article III, a 
party must demonstrate (1) injury in fact, (2) causation, and (3) redressability. Lujan 
v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 561-62 (1992). Each element must be supported 
“with the manner and degree of evidence required at the successive stages of the 
litigation.” Id. at 561. Here, the district court assessed futility under a standard that

assumes the truth of Applicants’ allegations. App. 88a-89a. Those allegations 
establish standing on precisely the logic Texas invoked, and the district court 
accepted, to establish Texas’s own injury and redressability.
1. The Cities’ standing follows from Texas’s own theory of 
standing

thereby inflicting a monetary harm. Both Columbus and Baltimore have local income

their applications are pending—now face reopened removal cases. Id. Each worker 
who is ultimately removed is a specific taxpayer whose payments the Cities lose. Id.

EPA, 606 U.S. 100, 114 (2025) (citation omitted). 
The district court held otherwise only by applying one standard to Texas and 
another to the Cities. It entered judgment on Texas’s allegation that vacatur “will

B. The Consent Judgment is Likely to Be Vacated
The consent judgment is indefensible. Texas sued, the government agreed, and 
the court entered judgment, all on the same day. App. 1a, 44a, 49a. That judgment 
was entered without a case or controversy and in circumvention of the APA, declares 
unauthorized a practice the INA authorizes, and grants relief that sweeps far beyond 
the harm Texas claimed.
1. The consent judgment was entered without a case or 
controversy
An Article III case or controversy requires parties with adverse legal interests 
who pursue “an honest and actual antagonistic assertion of rights.” Muskrat v. United 
States, 219 U.S. 346, 359 (1911) (quoting Chicago & G.T. Ry. Co. v. Wellman, 143 U.S. 
339, 345 (1892)). When “both litigants desire precisely the same result,” a federal 
court must dismiss the case. Moore v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Bd. of Educ., 402 U.S. 
47, 48 (1971) (per curiam); see also United States v. Johnson, 319 U.S. 302, 305 (1943)
(“Such a suit is collusive because it is not in any real sense adversary.”).
The adversity requirement is not a formality. Without it, a case becomes “a 
hobbled litigation rather than a full and fair adversarial testing” of the interests at 
stake. Berger, 597 U.S. at 192. That risk is most evident where, as here, the defendant 
does not merely concede but joins the plaintiff’s motion for judgment on the day suit 
is filed.
DOJ’s abandonment of the defenses it ordinarily presses confirms the absence 
of a genuine controversy. The government holds, and litigates, the position that the 
APA does not authorize universal vacatur—yet it told the district court it “agree[d]

27
not to pursue this position in this case,” while “reserv[ing] the right to continue to 
advance” it in others. App. 45a n.1. It likewise did not contend that Texas’s standing 
was insufficient, despite Texas’s theory of injury resembling the one rejected in 
United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670. DOJ abandoned those obvious defenses here 
because it had already announced it would not defend the Rule at all. App. 107a.
Because no case or controversy ever existed, the consent judgment is likely to 
be vacated for lack of Article III jurisdiction. See Local No. 93, Int’l Ass’n of 
Firefighters v. City of Cleveland, 478 U.S. 501, 525 (1986) (“[A] consent decree must 
spring from and serve to resolve a dispute within the court’s subject-matter 
jurisdiction.”).
2. The consent judgment circumvents the APA’s rulemaking 
requirements
The consent judgment also flouts the APA. A federal regulation adopted 
through notice-and-comment rulemaking can be rescinded only through notice-andcomment rulemaking. Mortg. Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. at 101. That process affords
affected parties the right to comment, 5 U.S.C. § 553(c), and to seek judicial review of 
any resulting rescission, see Dep’t of Com., 588 U.S. at 773-76. An agency cannot 
“circumvent” its notice-and-comment obligations “merely by confessing that the 
regulations were defective in some respect.” Consumer Energy Council, 673 F.2d at
447 n.79. DOJ appeared to concede as much below, U.S. 5th Cir. Opp. to Mot. to Stay 
15, consistent with its Office of Legal Counsel’s longstanding view that agencies “are 
not free in the course of litigation to . . . adopt a regulatory interpretation” that the 
APA requires be adopted “only through notice and comment rulemaking,” Authority

28
of the United States to Enter Settlements Limiting the Future Exercise of Executive 
Branch Discretion, 23 Op. O.L.C. 126, 129, 137 n.8 (1999). And Texas pressed the 
same argument in San Francisco, see S.F. Br. 3 (the government must “respect [a] 
duly enacted Rule until it repeals it through notice-and-comment rulemaking”).
Yet here, DOJ substituted “rulemaking-by-collusive-acquiescence.” City & 
County of San Francisco, 596 U.S. at 766 (Roberts, C.J., concurring) (citation and 
quotation marks omitted). Recognizing as much and invalidating the consent 
judgment on that basis would not compel the conclusion that the government can
never concede in appropriate circumstances that a regulation is unlawful. But the 
government surely cannot use manufactured litigation to circumvent the APA and to 
bind, in perpetuity, future administrations that do not share its policy preferences.
Cf. Horne, 557 U.S. at 449 (recognizing that “overbroad” consent decrees constrain 
public officers’ “ability to fulfill their duties as democratically-elected officials”). The 
sequence of events here demonstrates that this case falls into the latter category.
3. The INA authorizes administrative closure
The consent judgment’s central legal premise is that “no statute authorizes” 
administrative closure. App. 49a. The premise is wrong. The INA authorizes the 
Attorney General to adopt procedural rules like this one, and Congress preserved the 
closure authority EOIR was already exercising when it restructured the immigration 
agencies in 2002.
Congress charged the Attorney General with supervising the immigration 
adjudication system, see 8 U.S.C. § 1103(g)(1), and broadly authorized him to

29
“establish such regulations[] . . . as the Attorney General determines to be necessary 
for carrying out” his responsibilities under the Act, id. § 1103(g)(2). That authority 
comfortably encompasses procedural rules conducive to the fair and efficient 
functioning of the adjudication system—especially as to the many procedural matters 
the INA does not itself address. This Court has long held that “administrative 
agencies . . . will be in a better position than federal courts or Congress itself to design 
procedural rules adapted to the peculiarities of the industry and the tasks of the 
agency involved.” Vt. Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 435 
U.S. 519, 525 (1978) (quoting FCC v. Schreiber, 381 U.S. 279, 290 (1965)). That 
principle applies with full force to the agencies charged with conducting immigration 
proceedings. See, e.g., Mejia-Alvarenga v. Garland, 95 F.4th 319, 326 (5th Cir. 2024)
(“[B]ecause Congress has given the BIA the responsibility to conduct its own 
proceedings, the agency should be free to fashion its own rules of procedure[.]”
(cleaned up)). 
The Rule exercises that authority to provide procedural rules governing 
administrative closure. Even the 2020 Rule, which the consent judgment revives, 
rests on that understanding. It bars administrative closure “unless a regulation 
promulgated by the Department of Justice or a previous judicially approved 
settlement expressly authorizes such an action.” 85 Fed. Reg. 81588, 81651, 81655 
(Dec. 16, 2020).
Congress also expressly preserved the administrative closure authority that 
EOIR was exercising. The Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA) carried forward for

30
the Attorney General “such authorities and functions under [the INA] relating to the 
immigration and naturalization of [noncitizens] as were exercised by [EOIR], or by 
the Attorney General with respect to [EOIR],” prior to the Act. HSA § 1102, 116 Stat. 
2135, 2274; 8 U.S.C. § 1103(g)(1); see 6 U.S.C. § 521. Immigration judges and the BIA 
had used administrative closure to manage congested dockets since at least the 
1980s, see Arcos Sanchez v. Att’y Gen., 997 F.3d 113, 116-17 (3d Cir. 2021); Appellate 
Procedures and Decisional Finality in Immigration Proceedings; Administrative 
Closure, 88 Fed. Reg. 62242, 62243-46 (Sept. 8, 2023), and the Attorney General had 
issued regulations directing administrative closure in specified circumstances years 
before the HSA’s enactment, see 8 C.F.R. § 245.13(d)(3)(i) (2011), as added by 63 Fed. 
Reg. 27823, 27829 (May 21, 1998); 8 C.F.R. § 245.15(p)(4), as added by 64 Fed. Reg. 
25756, 25771 (May 12, 1999).
The district court considered none of this. It received no adversarial briefing 
and entered judgment the day Texas sued. App. 1a, 49a. Its declaration rests on a 
single decision from a different circuit, Hernandez-Serrano v. Barr, 981 F.3d 459 (6th 
Cir. 2020). But Hernandez-Serrano considered a distinct question: whether a prior 
version of EOIR’s regulations—which authorized adjudicators to take any action 
“necessary or appropriate for the disposition” of a case, 8 C.F.R. § 1003.10(b)—
conferred general authority to close cases administratively. The court held it did not, 
because administrative closure “is not itself a ‘disposition.’” 981 F.3d at 463. The Sixth 
Circuit did not construe the INA, and it did not consider the validity of the Rule at 
issue here. The Sixth Circuit itself later recognized that immigration judges may

31
administratively close cases in at least some circumstances. Garcia-DeLeon, 999 F.3d 
at 991-93. Hernandez-Serrano does not support the consent judgment, even assuming 
it was correctly decided. But see, e.g., Meza Morales, 973 F.3d at 667 (upholding 
administrative closure under the prior EOIR regulations). Accordingly, the district 
court’s judgment lacks any authority supporting its newfound interpretation of 
federal law.
4. The consent judgment sweeps far beyond anything Texas 
challenged
The consent judgment also grants relief no injury could support. It vacates 
provisions of the Rule that Texas never challenged, and it enjoins rulemakings that 
have not yet occurred. App. 49a-50a. Neither form of relief can stand.
1. The judgment vacates the entire Rule. Yet Texas’s claims target only the 
Rule’s administrative-closure provisions. See App. 30a-31a, 42a, 49a-50a. The Rule 
does much more, and those other provisions are severable.
A “two-prong inquiry” governs whether a regulation is severable: (1) “the intent 
of the agency” and (2) “whether the remainder of the regulation could function 
sensibly without the stricken provisions.” Texas v. United States, 126 F.4th 392, 419 
(5th Cir. 2025) (cleaned up); see also K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 486 U.S. 281, 294 
(1988). Both factors point the same way here. The Rule’s severability clause provides 
that, if any portion is “held invalid by a court, the Department intends for all other 
parts of the rule that are capable of operating in the absence of the specific portion 
that has been invalidated to remain in effect.” 89 Fed. Reg. at 46786. And the 
remaining provisions can so operate. “[A]dministrative closure and termination are

32
two separate procedural tools that operate independently of each other,” and the 
Rule’s changes to BIA procedures—“such as to briefing schedules, background checks, 
sua sponte reopening and reconsideration, and adjudication timelines, among 
others”—function independently of administrative closure. Id. Vacating them 
redresses no injury Texas alleged.
2. The injunction—which indefinitely bars future administrations from 
exercising their regulatory authority to propose and adopt a new regulation 
addressing administrative closure—is even worse. It bars the government “from 
promulgating regulations that permit immigration judges the authority to 
administratively close removal proceedings without reaching the merits of a case 
absent an express statutory basis to do so.” App. 50a. Texas cannot be injured by a 
regulation that does not exist. And a claim resting on “contingent future events that 
may not occur as anticipated, or indeed may not occur at all,” is not ripe. Texas v. 
United States, 523 U.S. 296, 300 (1998) (cleaned up). On the federal government’s 
urging, this Court recently held that a state’s standing cannot rest on a “string of 
speculations” about the content of a future rulemaking. Trump v. California, 609 U.S. 
___, 2026 WL 2473573, at *4 (U.S. Aug. 24, 2026) (per curiam). Any injunction must 
“be limited to the inadequacy that produced the injury in fact,” which extends (at 
most) to the Rule, not to rulemakings no one has proposed. Lewis v. Casey, 518 U.S. 
343, 357 (1996).
Even setting aside that jurisdictional defect, the injunction is unnecessary. If 
vacatur alone is “sufficient to redress [the plaintiff’s] injury, no recourse to the

33
additional and extraordinary relief of an injunction [is] warranted.” Monsanto Co. v. 
Geertson Seed Farms, 561 U.S. 139, 166 (2010). No party showed, and the district 
court did not find, that an injunction was necessary under the traditional equitable 
factors. See App. 46a, 50a. 
III. A STAY IS NECESSARY TO AVOID IRREPARABLE INJURY BOTH TO 
APPLICANTS AND THE PUBLIC INTEREST
The consent judgment inflicts irreparable injury on each Applicant. For Centro 
Legal, the judgment is poised to return 80 to 100 of its administratively closed cases 
to active dockets, each requiring 40 to 200 hours of uncompensated additional work. 
App. 63a-65a. Centro Legal will be “forced to devote thousands of hours” to litigating 
cases that had been closed. App. 71a. The Cities’ injury is equally irreversible. Each 
crime victim who does not come forward, stops cooperating, or is removed midprosecution, cannot testify, and the case against the offender collapses. See App. 75a, 
83a. Those harms to the Cities’ “law enforcement and public safety interests” are 
plainly irreparable. Maryland v. King, 567 U.S. 1301, 1303 (2012) (Roberts, C.J., in 
chambers). The Cities will also lose taxpayers. Columbus and Baltimore levy local 
income taxes, including on immigrants who have work authorization while their 
removal cases are administratively closed. App. 53a, 81a-82a. Each taxpayer removed 
permanently deprives the Cities of revenue. See Ala. Ass’n of Realtors v. Dep’t of 
Health & Hum. Servs., 594 U.S. 758, 765 (2021) (crediting lost “rent payments with 
no guarantee of eventual recovery” as irreparable harm).
The balance of equities favors a stay. A stay would restore the status quo that 
prevailed for more than two years. The Rule was promulgated in May 2024, and Texas

34
did not challenge it until June 2026. App. 1a. Whatever costs Texas attributes to the 
Rule, it shouldered them for two years before suing; a few more months while the 
appeal proceeds will not tip the balance. Nor would a stay burden the federal 
government. EOIR itself instructed its adjudicators that, “until it is rescinded, 
superseded, enjoined, vacated, or otherwise determined to be unlawful,” the Rule 
remains “binding on EOIR adjudicators.” App. 107a. A stay asks nothing more of 
them, and it leaves the government free to rescind the Rule through notice-andcomment rulemaking, as the APA has always required.
The public interest unmistakably weighs in Applicants’ favor. For example, 
some removals spurred by the consent judgment are permanent. A child qualifying 
for special immigrant juvenile status, see 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(27)(J), who is removed 
before a visa becomes available will be deprived of their ability to adjust status, 
because adjustment requires physical presence in the United States. App. 65a. The 
consent judgment exposes such children, and many others whose cases were 
administratively closed, to that fate in a practice that, by the parties’ own account, 
has reached hundreds of thousands of cases. App. 46a. It does so on the strength of a 
judgment that never received adversarial testing. If the judgment remains in force 
while Applicants’ appeal proceeds, it will stand as a working template for any 
administration that wishes to repeal a regulation without notice and comment. 
This Court has not hesitated to stay lower-court orders that set aside federal 
policies nationwide. See, e.g., Trump v. CASA, Inc., 606 U.S. 831 (2025); Trump v.
Orr, 146 S. Ct. 44 (2025). The Rule was lawfully promulgated through notice and

35
comment, and the current administration’s disfavor does not entitle it to less respect 
than any other regulation. And this Court granted a stay in Mayorkas to keep a 
vacatur from taking effect while it considered whether would-be intervenors could 
defend the vacated policy. 143 S. Ct. at 478. The case for that relief is yet stronger 
here. 
CONCLUSION
The Court should stay the consent judgment pending the Fifth Circuit’s 
disposition of Applicants’ appeal and, if necessary, the disposition of a timely petition 
for a writ of certiorari.

The “Administrative Closure Rule”
9. The regulation codified at 8 C.F.R. § 1003.18 is titled “Docket management” and 
sets forth subsections titled “Scheduling,” “Notice,” “Administrative closure and recalendaring,” 
and “Termination.” The order and final judgment issued in this case on June 22, 2026 references 
the final rule titled “Efficient Case and Docket Management in Immigration Proceedings,” 
promulgated at 89 Fed. Reg. 46,742, and proceeds to refer to this rule as “the Administrative 
Closure Rule.” It then vacates “the Administrative Closure Rule” and enjoins the Department of 
Justice from promulgating regulations that permit administrative closure of removal proceedings, 
absent express statutory authority. 
10. At least one Immigration Judge in the San Francisco Immigration Court has raised 
the question sua sponte whether he has authority to terminate—not only administratively close—
removal proceedings following the District Court’s order in this case. Therefore, the Court’s order 
may and will be read to vacate the entire rule now codified at 8 C.F.R. § 1003.18, not simply the 
provision governing administrative closure.

How Vacatur Will Harm Centro Legal 
19. The vacatur of the rule codified at 8 C.F.R. § 1003.18(c) will irreparably harm

compounding challenges that would make it prohibitively costly to serve our clients meaningfully.

mandatory or discretionary termination whose removal proceedings remain on the Immigration 
Court’s active docket, assuming the Department of Homeland Security reads the June 22nd 
decision to eliminate § 1003.18(d) pertaining to termination, I predict that it will recommence 
removal proceedings for those clients whose cases were terminated pursuant to subsection 
(d)(1)(ii) (permitting discretionary termination for unaccompanied children with pending TVPRA 
asylum applications as well as noncitizens who are prima facie eligible for lawful status before 
USCIS). I estimate that this will propel at least 50 Centro Legal clients back into removal 
proceedings. With respect to administrative closure, as noted above, I estimate that we currently 
carry 80-100 administratively closed cases. Once proceedings recommence or are recalendared for

II. LEGLA STANDARD 
A. Article III Standing
Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction and must have “statutory or constitutional 
power to adjudicate the case.” Home Builders Ass’n of Miss. v. City of Madison, 143 F.3d 1006, 
1010 (5th Cir. 1998). “Under the Constitution’s Article III cases and controversies requirement, a 
plaintiff must establish standing to sue. Standing requires: (1) an injury in fact, (2) a sufficient 
‘causal connection between the injury and the conduct complained of’ and (3) a likelihood that the 
injury will be redressed by a favorable decision.” Morgan v. Huntington Ingalls, Inc., 879 F.3d 
602, 606 (5th Cir. 2018) (quoting Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560–61 (1992); U.S.
CONST. art. III, § 2. The injury cannot be merely “conjectural or hypothetical.” Summers v. Earth 
Island Inst., 555 U.S. 488, 493 (2009). Causation requires that the injury “fairly can be traced to 
the challenged action of the defendant” rather than to “the independent action of some third party 
not before the court.” Simon v. E. Ky. Welfare Rts. Org., 426 U.S. 26, 41–42 (1976).
When a motion to intervene is opposed and the proposed pleading advances defenses no 
existing party asserts, the Court must first determine whether the proposed intervention is futile. 
United States v. Texas, 181 F.4th 548, 553–54 (5th Cir. 2026). The Rule 12(b)(6) standard applies: 
factual allegations are assumed true, the pleading is construed liberally. Id. Futility is a threshold 
inquiry that precedes the factors in Rule 24(a) and (b), and it applies to proposed defense-side 
intervenors. Id. An intervenor that alone seeks appellate relief must independently demonstrate a

B. Intervention as of Right
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(a) requires that a party be permitted to intervene in an 
action if it shows by “timely motion” that (a) “it has a protectable ‘interest’ in the action,” (b) “the 
‘disposing of the action’ could ‘impair’ its ability to protect that interest,” and (c) “existing parties 
do not ‘adequately represent’ that interest.” Louisiana v. Burgum, 132 F.4th 918, 922 (5th Cir. 
2025) (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 24(a)(2)). “Failure to satisfy any one requirement precludes 
intervention of right.” Haspel & Davis Milling & Planting Co. v. Bd. of Levee Comm’rs of the 
Orleans Levee Dist., 493 F.3d 570, 578 (5th Cir. 2007). “Although the movant bears the burden 
of establishing its right to intervene, Rule 24 is to be liberally construed.” Wal-Mart Stores, Inc . 
v. Tex. Alcoholic Beverage Comm’n, 834 F.3d 562, 565 (5th Cir. 2016).

I. Introduction
On November 22, 2021, the EOIR Director issued Director’s Memorandum (DM) 22-03, 
Administrative Closure, purporting to provide guidance regarding the use of administrative closure
by EOIR adjudicators. A subsequent rulemaking superseded that DM, see Efficient Case and 
Docket Management in Immigration Proceedings, 89 FR 46742 (May 29, 2024) (ECDM Rule), 
and rendered it unnecessary. Furthermore, many of the assertions in that DM were either factually 
or legally dubious, and EOIR cannot defend it as a policy. Consequently, it warrants rescission 
and cancellation. 
II. History of EOIR’s Use of Administrative Closure 
No statute authorizes administrative closure by EOIR adjudicators, and prior to the ECDM Rule, 
no regulation clearly authorized it either. EOIR’s use of administrative closure in immigration 
proceedings dates back to at least the 1970s, as EOIR still has unresolved cases that were
administratively closed during that decade. The use of administrative closure became more 
widespread in the 1980s following the issuance of an Operating Policies and Procedures 
Memorandum (“OPPM”) in 1984 setting forth options available to Immigration Judges in cases 
where aliens failed to appear for their hearings, including the option to administratively close 
cases. OPPM 84-2: Cases in Which Respondents/Applicants Fail to Appear for Hearing (Mar. 7, 
1984) (rescinded). Notably, that OPPM did not identify any basis for its authority, and there was 
no delegation by the Attorney General of such authority. 
Subsequently, the use of administrative closure generally tended to correspond with either 
legislative changes providing new statutory forms of relief for aliens or with federal court 
settlement agreements requiring its use. For example, in 1986, shortly after the passage of the 
Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, creating an amnesty program for certain illegal

III. Inaccurate Characterizations of Administrative Closure 
EOIR’s increased utilization of administrative closure as a policy-driven tool since 2011 also 
corresponded with repeated—yet demonstrably untrue—assertions about its usage. These 
knowing mischaracterizations of administrative closure, particularly by those with access to 
accurate information, warrant significant rectification. 
For example, administrative closure has often been described as a temporary measure. See, e.g., 
Matter of Gutierrez-Lopez, 21 I&N Dec. 479, 480 (BIA 1996) (“Administrative closure of a case 
is used to temporarily remove a case from an Immigration Judge’s calendar or from the Board’s 
docket.”), overruled by Matter of Avetisyan, 25 I&N Dec. at 697. Although that may have been 
arguably true in the 1980s or 1990s, it is no longer considered a temporary measure. On the 
contrary, the average length of time that a case is administratively closed at the immigration court 
level is approximately 15 years, and approximately 29 years at the Board level. These averages 
do not reflect “temporary” action by any reasonable definition of the term. Rather, administrative
closure is more properly characterized as an indeterminate or unbounded measure, which typically 
stops an adjudication indefinitely. 
Second, administrative closure is often erroneously alleged to aid docket management and has 
been described as an “administrative convenience,” Matter of Amico, 19 I&N Dec. at 654 n.1. Yet, 
periods of increased usage of administrative closure have also corresponded to periods of 
significant increases to EOIR’s backlog. For instance, between January 2013 and January 2017, 
the number of administratively closed cases increased from nearly 172,000 to over 268,000; over 
that same time period, EOIR’s backlog increased from just under 550,000 cases to nearly 859,000. 
Similarly, between January 2021 and January 2025, the number of administratively closed cases 
increased from nearly 278,000 to almost 392,000; over that same time period, EOIR’s backlog 
increased from approximately 1.68 million cases to over 4.1 million cases. Indeed, EOIR’s 
experience shows that increased usage of administrative closure leads to greater lost-docket time
as parties debate whether it is appropriate in a particular case, leading to even more continuances 
while that issue is resolved, and, if administrative closure is not ordered, a lengthy delay occurs in 
adjudicating the merits of a case that otherwise would have been decided much earlier. Moreover, 
as a matter of logic, because administrative closure does not dispose of a case, it cannot help 
manage the overall docket; rather, it simply delays a case indefinitely without a disposition so that 
it remains in a liminal state. Administrative closure merely “kicks the can down the road,” 
increasing the overall backlog while leaving ripple effects—e.g. multiple continuances and lost

IV. Additional Legal Questions Surrounding the Use of Administrative Closure
In addition to overriding DHS’s prosecutorial discretion, violating basic administrative separationof-functions principles, and the failure in Matter of Avetisyan to explain or acknowledge its 
departure from prior Board precedent, EOIR’s use of administrative closure, including as codified 
by the ECDM Rule, presents several other problematic legal questions. 
First, EOIR’s widespread use of administrative closure, to the extent that cases may be closed for 
decades, creates a serious tension with—if not also a direct violation of—EOIR’s regulations 
requiring cases to be adjudicated in a timely manner. See, e.g., 8 C.F.R. § 1003.10(b) (“[i]n all 
cases, immigration judges shall seek to resolve the questions before them in a timely and impartial 
manner”). Further, the lack of timely adjudication of approximately 400,000 cases places EOIR 
at great risk of an onslaught of mandamus petitions. See 28 U.S.C. § 1361. Put simply—and also 
as a matter of good governance—“[a]n adjudicatory default on that scale strikes directly at the rule 
of law,” Hernandez-Serrano v. Barr, 981 F.3d 459, 461 (6th Cir. 2020), and EOIR’s “adjudicatory 
default” due to administrative closure over a long period of time potentially jeopardizes the 
agency’s ability to defend itself from legal challenges.

More troublingly, EOIR’s use of administrative closure, including the ECDM Rule, appears to 
implicate the major questions doctrine. As discussed, supra, the use of administrative closure has 
effectively become an amnesty program, allowing otherwise illegal aliens to remain in the United 
States indefinitely—and typically with the benefit of work authorization—without the threat of 
removal. However, there is absolutely no statutory authorization for such a program, as there is 
no such authorization for administrative closure in the first instance. Moreover, as also noted
elsewhere, even the regulatory and adjudicatory bases for it are on questionable administrative law 
footing. EOIR’s assertion of heretofore unknown regulatory authority for the widespread use of 
administrative closure is of recent vintage and conspicuously fails to assert any statutory basis. 
Rather, it is a transformative expansion of its authority in order to create a de facto amnesty 
program for hundreds of thousands of aliens. The absence of any statutory basis for such a 
program—even beyond the dubious regulatory or adjudicatory basis for it—raises serious 
separation-of-powers or nondelegation issues for EOIR and squarely implicates the major 
questions doctrine. 
Although “the major questions ‘label’ may be relatively recent, it refers to an identifiable body of 
law that has developed over a series of significant cases spanning decades.” Biden v. Nebraska, 
600 U.S. 477, 504-05 (2023) (cleaned up). As commonly understood, the major questions doctrine 
requires Congress to have spoken clearly to the assignment of certain authorities to administrative 
agencies, especially those purporting to address questions “of vast economic and political 
significance.” Alabama Ass’n of Realtors v. Dept. of Health and Hum. Servs., 594 U.S. 758, 764 
(2021) (cleaned up). Put more clearly, 
[t]he major questions doctrine serves a similar function [as the nondelegation 
doctrine] by guarding against unintentional, oblique, or otherwise unlikely 
delegations of the legislative power. Sometimes, Congress passes broadly worded 
statutes seeking to resolve important policy questions in a field while leaving an 
agency to work out the details of implementation. Later, the agency may seek to 
exploit some gap, ambiguity, or doubtful expression in Congress’s statutes to 
assume responsibilities far beyond its initial assignment. The major questions 
doctrine guards against this possibility by recognizing that Congress does not 
usually “hide elephants in mouseholes.” In this way, the doctrine is a vital check 
on expansive and aggressive assertions of executive authority. 
NFIB v. OSHA, 595 U.S. 109, 125 (2022) (Gorsuch, J., concurring) (cleaned up). The doctrine 
applies “when an agency claims the power to resolve a matter of great political significance or end 
an earnest and profound debate across the country.” West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 743 
(2022) (Gorsuch, J., concurring) (cleaned up). 
There is no question that immigration, particularly a de facto amnesty, is a matter of “great political 
significance” and subject to “an earnest and profound debate” across the United States. It is 
equally clear that EOIR has seized for itself an authority to indefinitely suspend cases without a 
disposition, administrative closure, that has no statutory basis at all. That combination—i.e. using 
an authority to effectuate amnesty to hundreds of thousands of otherwise removable aliens without 
any statutory basis—squarely implicates the major questions doctrine, as Congress has not clearly

Whether EOIR’s use of administrative closure as a de facto amnesty program definitively violates 
the major questions doctrine is beyond the scope of this Policy Memorandum (PM).4 Nevertheless, 
that question further underscores the myriad of problems EOIR’s use of administrative closure, 
codified in the ECDM Rule, has engendered. At best, the ECDM Rule appears arbitrary and 
capricious because it wholly failed to consider several problematic aspects of administrative 
closure5 and was wholly contrary to the evidence that administrative closure is neither temporary 
nor is an effective docket management tool. See, e.g., Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of U.S., Inc. v. 
State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (“Normally, an agency rule would be 
arbitrary and capricious if the agency. . .entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the 
problem [or], offered an explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the 
agency. . .”). At worst, it may be ultra vires or unconstitutional in violation of the major questions 
doctrine because it arrogated to EOIR an authority to grant amnesty to hundreds of thousands of 
illegal aliens without any statutory basis whatsoever. As such, EOIR could not—and will not—
defend the ECDM Rule in good faith against legal challenge. Nevertheless, until it is rescinded, 
superseded, enjoined, vacated, or otherwise determined to be unlawful, the changes made by that 
rulemaking remain binding on EOIR adjudicators. Accordingly, this PM cannot—and does not 
purport to—alter that rulemaking’s legal effect, and adjudicators should continue to adhere to it 
unless they have a legal basis for not doing so. 
V. Conclusion 
EOIR’s use of administrative closure, particularly between 2011 and 2017 and between 2021 and 
2025, was an unmitigated disaster from a policy standpoint and strongly appears to have also been 
unlawful. Further, not only did it constitute “[a]n adjudicatory default. . .[that] strikes directly at 
the rule of law,” Hernandez-Serrano, 981 F.3d at 461, but in EOIR’s experience, it contributed to 
significant increases in EOIR’s adjudicatory backlog. To the extent DM 22-03 contributed to that 
“adjudicatory default” it merits cancellation and rescission even if it had not otherwise been 
effectively superseded by the ECDM Rule, and EOIR’s “adjudicatory default” due to 
administrative closure over a long period of time potentially jeopardizes the agency’s ability to 
defend itself from legal challenges. Accordingly, DM 22-03 is cancelled and rescinded.
